title: Installation
text:
Setting up commenting takes about ten minutes, once. You need:
Steps 2 and 3 are done once. After that, one relay serves every site you add, and another site takes a couple of minutes.

title: Installation
text:
What readers will see
A reader highlights a passage and clicks 💬 Comment:

They type their name and comment, and read who will post it and what becomes public:

They check the issue exactly as it will be posted:

And they get a link to the issue:

The rest of this page sets that up.

title: Installation
text:
1. Install the extension
In a terminal, in your Quarto project’s folder (the one with _quarto.yml), run:
quarto add VagishHemmige/quarto-commenting-extension
Answer Y when it asks to confirm. It adds the extension under _extensions/. Commit that folder with your site.

title: Installation
text:
2. Create a GitHub App
A GitHub App is a GitHub account that belongs to the relay rather than to you. Issues it creates show as posted by a bot, such as jdoe-comments[bot], so reader comments are easy to tell apart from your own, and GitHub notifies you of them as it would of anyone else’s. The app is allowed to do one thing, work with issues, and only in the repositories you install it on.

Open GitHub’s form for a new app: https://github.com/settings/apps/new. To get there by clicking instead, use your profile picture → Settings (your account’s settings, not a repository’s), then Developer settings at the bottom of the left sidebar, then GitHub Apps → New GitHub App.
GitHub App name: something like “jdoe-comments”. The name has to be unused across all of GitHub, and it is what readers’ issues will show as posted by.
Homepage URL: your site’s address, or your GitHub profile. It is required but not used.
Webhook: untick Active. The relay only sends to GitHub; it never needs GitHub to call it.
Permissions → Repository permissions → Issues: choose Read and write. Leave everything else at No access. GitHub adds Metadata: Read-only itself.
Where can this GitHub App be installed? Choose Only on this account, then click Create GitHub App.
On the app’s page that opens, note the App ID near the top. Scroll to Private keys and click Generate a private key. A .pem file downloads. You will paste its contents into the relay in step 3, and you can then delete the file.
Click Install App in the left sidebar, then Install. Choose Only select repositories, pick the repository that will receive comments, and click Install.

Why so narrow? The relay accepts comments from anyone on the internet, so what the app can do is the limit on any damage. Even if the private key leaked, it could only create and edit issues, as the bot, in the repositories the app is installed on. It could not touch your code or post as you. See Security and privacy.

title: Installation
section: 3. Create the relay in Google Apps Script
text:
3. Create the relay in Google Apps Script
The relay is a small script in your own Google account. It holds the app’s key, checks each comment, works out which repository it is for, and creates the issue.

Go to https://script.google.com and click New project. Rename it “issue-comments” by clicking “Untitled project” at the top.
Open Code.gs as plain text, select all and copy. In the script editor, delete everything in Code.gs, paste, and click the save icon.
Click the gear icon (Project Settings) in the left sidebar. Under Script Properties, click Add script property and add:



Property
Value




GITHUB_APP_ID
the App ID from step 2


GITHUB_APP_KEY
the whole private key: open the .pem file in a text editor, copy everything including the -----BEGIN and -----END lines, and paste. It doesn’t matter if the line breaks disappear.


GITHUB_OWNER
your GitHub user name. A page at https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ sends its comments to <owner>/<repo>.


PASSCODE
optional: a passcode readers must enter. See Options.



Then click Save script properties. If your site is not at https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/, also add REPO_MAP (see Options). The other optional properties are there too.
Click Deploy → New deployment. Click the gear next to “Select type” and choose Web app. Set Execute as: Me and Who has access: Anyone, and click Deploy.
Authorize when asked. Google says “Google hasn’t verified this app”, because the script is yours rather than a published app. Click Advanced → Go to issue-comments (unsafe), then Allow.
Copy the Web app URL. It starts https://script.google.com/macros/s/ and ends in /exec. To find it again later, use Deploy → Manage deployments. Don’t use a URL ending in /dev.
Open the URL in a browser tab. It should show {"ok":true,"message":"issue-comments relay is running."}.

title: Installation
text:
4. Turn it on in Quarto
Add this to _quarto.yml for the whole site, or to one page’s front matter for just that page, using your /exec URL:
filters:
  - issue-comments

issue-comments:
  endpoint: https://script.google.com/macros/s/XXXXXXXX/exec
  owner: Jane Doe
  contact: mailto:jane@example.com
  passcode: true   # only if you set PASSCODE in step 3

Put both at the top level of _quarto.yml, not under website: or format:.
owner is the name readers are told the issue is posted on behalf of. contact is where they go to change or remove a comment: an email link, a contact page or your GitHub profile.
Any wording readers see can be changed with a text: block; see Options.
If you already have a filters: list, add - issue-comments to it rather than starting a second one:


Starting with one page is the cautious choice: once it’s on in _quarto.yml, every page shows the Comment button.

title: Installation
text:
5. Publish and test
Render and publish the site the way you usually do. Commit all of the extension’s files with it, not just some:

Then open the published page, highlight a sentence, click 💬 Comment and post. The issue should appear in your repository with the reader-comment label, posted by your app’s bot.

title: Installation
text:
If something doesn’t work

The dialog says “Comments are not accepted from this page.”

The relay couldn’t match the page to a repository the app is installed on. Check that the page’s address is https://<GITHUB_OWNER>.github.io/<repo>/… (or is in REPO_MAP), and that the app is installed on that repository: profile picture → Settings → Applications → Installed GitHub Apps → Configure. This always happens in quarto preview, whose pages are on your own computer, unless you add the preview address to REPO_MAP; see Options.

The dialog says “That passcode is not correct.”

The relay has PASSCODE set. If the page shows no passcode box, add passcode: true to the page’s issue-comments: block.

The dialog says “Something went wrong.”

Most often the app: GITHUB_APP_ID is wrong, GITHUB_APP_KEY is incomplete, or the app lacks Issues: Read and write. The error itself is in Apps Script under Executions.

The dialog says “Commenting is not configured yet.”

GITHUB_APP_ID or GITHUB_APP_KEY is missing from Script Properties.

There is no Comment button.

Check that issue-comments is in filters:, that the issue-comments: block has an endpoint, and that the _extensions/ folder is committed if your site is rendered on GitHub. Quarto prints a warning when it renders a page whose issue-comments: block has no endpoint.

Posting shows an error such as “Failed to fetch”.

The page couldn’t reach the relay. Check that endpoint is the /exec URL and that the deployment’s access is Anyone.

title: Installation
text:
Adding another site
One relay serves every repository the app is installed on, so a new site needs no new script:

App. Add the new repository to the app: profile picture → Settings → Applications → Installed GitHub Apps, then Configure next to your app, add the repository under Repository access, and Save.
Site. Install the extension in the new site (step 1) and turn it on (step 4) with the same endpoint.

If the new site’s address isn’t https://<GITHUB_OWNER>.github.io/<repo>/, or its comments should go to a different repository than its own, add it to REPO_MAP too.

title: Installation
section: Moving an older relay to the app
text:
Moving an older relay to the app
Relays set up before version 0.3.0 posted with a personal token and served one site each. To move one over without changing its /exec URL:

Create and install the app (step 2), on every repository your sites send comments to.
In the existing relay’s Script Properties, add GITHUB_APP_ID, GITHUB_APP_KEY and GITHUB_OWNER (and REPO_MAP if needed). Keep the old ones for now.
Replace the script with the new Code.gs, save, and use Deploy → Manage deployments → Edit → Version: New version → Deploy. This keeps the URL.
Post a test comment from each site. Once they work, delete GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_REPO and SITE_PREFIX from Script Properties, and revoke the old token on GitHub under Developer settings → Personal access tokens.
Sites that had their own relays can switch their endpoint to this one. Then delete the extra Apps Script projects.

title: 1. Manifest
text: The manifest tells Quarto that _extensions/issue-comments/ is an extension and that what it contributes is one filter.

title: 1. Manifest
text:
What each field does

title, author and version are shown by quarto add and quarto list extensions. The version here should match the one the filter gives its HTML dependency (see the Lua filter), so the browser does not keep a cached copy of an older script.
quarto-required: ">=1.4.0" makes Quarto refuse to run the extension on an older version rather than fail partway through. The filter relies on Quarto’s Lua API (quarto.doc.add_html_dependency, quarto.doc.include_text, quarto.json.encode and quarto.log.warning), so this floor should be raised if the filter starts using anything newer.
contributes: filters lists one Lua filter. A site turns it on by naming the extension, issue-comments, under filters:; Quarto then finds this manifest and runs issue-comments.lua.

Nothing else is declared. The JavaScript and CSS are not listed here because the filter attaches them itself, and only to HTML pages that have commenting configured.

title: 1. Manifest
text:
What quarto add installs
quarto add VagishHemmige/quarto-commenting-extension copies every folder under the repository’s _extensions/, so this folder must stay the only one there. That is why this website’s own tools live in site-tools/ rather than _extensions/.

title: 4. Styles
text: The stylesheet gives the buttons and dialog a look that fits the site. Every class starts with ic-, so it cannot clash with the site’s own styles.

title: 4. Styles
text:
Following the site’s theme
Colours come from the Bootstrap variables that Quarto’s HTML themes define (--bs-body-bg, --bs-primary and so on), each with a fallback. So the buttons and dialog take on the site’s theme, including a dark theme, and still look reasonable on a page without Bootstrap.

2. Lua filter
text: The filter runs once for each page Quarto renders. It decides whether the page gets commenting, settles the settings, and adds the script, the styles and the settings to the page. It does not change the page’s content.

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
The settings it accepts
The comment at the top of the file is the reference for the issue-comments: block. Only endpoint is required.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 1–13
-- issue-comments: let readers highlight text and send a comment that is
-- filed as a GitHub issue by a Google Apps Script relay.
--
-- issue-comments:
--   endpoint: https://script.google.com/macros/s/XXXX/exec   # required
--   owner: Jane Doe              # who posts the issues; defaults to `author`
--   contact: https://...         # how readers reach you (URL or mailto:)
--   preview: true                # show the exact issue before posting
--   passcode: false              # ask readers for a shared passcode
--   page-button: false           # also show "Comment on this page"
--   text:                        # optional: replace any wording readers see
--     heading: Comment on the draft
--     notice: "Comments go to {owner}'s team as GitHub issues. {contact}."

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
Reading YAML values
Quarto hands settings to a filter as Pandoc values, not plain strings: owner: Jane Doe arrives as a list of words. str turns any value into text, and treats an empty value as missing so that contact: "" behaves like no contact at all.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 15–20
local function str(v)
  if v == nil then return nil end
  local s = pandoc.utils.stringify(v)
  if s == "" then return nil end
  return s
end

bool gives each on/off setting its default when it is absent. YAML true arrives as a Lua boolean, but a value written as a string ("yes", "true") is accepted too.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 22–27
local function bool(v, default)
  if v == nil then return default end
  if type(v) == "boolean" then return v end
  local s = pandoc.utils.stringify(v)
  return s == "true" or s == "yes"
end

first_author provides the default owner. In Quarto, author can be written as a single name, a list of names, or a list of maps with a name field (the form most templates use); this takes the first name in any of the three.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 59–64
local function first_author(meta)
  local a = meta["author"]
  if type(a) == "table" and a[1] ~= nil then a = a[1] end
  if type(a) == "table" and a["name"] ~= nil then a = a["name"] end
  return str(a)
end

text_settings reads the text: block. It keeps only the keys the browser script uses, turns each value into a plain string, and warns about any other key, so a misspelt headng: is reported rather than silently ignored. The list of keys must match DEFAULT_TEXT in the browser script.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 29–35
-- Keys of `text:` the browser script uses; see DEFAULT_TEXT in issue-comments.js.
local TEXT_KEYS = {
  "button", "page-button", "heading", "preview-heading", "section",
  "name-label", "comment-label", "passcode-label", "notice", "contact-link",
  "preview-intro", "cancel", "edit", "close", "preview", "post", "posting",
  "thanks", "issue-link",
}


_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 38–56
local function text_settings(t)
  if t == nil then return nil end
  if type(t) ~= "table" then
    quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: `text` should be a map of wording to replace.")
    return nil
  end
  local known = {}
  for _, k in ipairs(TEXT_KEYS) do known[k] = true end
  local out, any = {}, false
  for k, v in pairs(t) do
    if not known[k] then
      quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: unknown `text` key `" .. tostring(k) .. "`; it is ignored.")
    else
      local s = str(v)
      if s ~= nil then out[k] = s; any = true end
    end
  end
  return any and out or nil
end

title: 2. Lua filter
section: Deciding whether the page gets commenting
text:
Deciding whether the page gets commenting
The work happens in Meta, which Pandoc calls once with the page’s metadata. It returns early, leaving the page unchanged, for any non-HTML output, so PDF and Word renders of the same source are untouched.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 67–69
if not quarto.doc.is_format("html") then
  return meta
end

A page with no issue-comments: block, or with issue-comments: false, is also left alone. That is how a page can opt out of a site-wide setting. A block that is not a map (for example issue-comments: true) is a mistake, so it produces a warning rather than silently doing nothing.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 71–78
local cfg = meta["issue-comments"]
if cfg == nil or cfg == false then
  return meta
end
if type(cfg) ~= "table" then
  quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: expected a map with at least `endpoint`.")
  return meta
end

Without an endpoint there is nowhere to send comments, so the page is left alone with a warning.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 80–84
local endpoint = str(cfg["endpoint"])
if endpoint == nil then
  quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: no `endpoint` set; commenting is disabled.")
  return meta
end

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
Settling the settings
These are the seven values the browser script receives. The keys are camel case (pageButton) because they become JavaScript properties; the text keys stay as written, since the script looks them up by those names. A missing contact is allowed, since readers are still told who to contact, but Quarto warns because they would have no link to follow.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 86–97
local settings = {
  endpoint = endpoint,
  owner = str(cfg["owner"]) or first_author(meta),
  contact = str(cfg["contact"]),
  preview = bool(cfg["preview"], true),
  passcode = bool(cfg["passcode"], false),
  pageButton = bool(cfg["page-button"], false),
  text = text_settings(cfg["text"]),
}
if settings.contact == nil then
  quarto.log.warning("issue-comments: no `contact` set; readers won't see how to reach you.")
end

title: 2. Lua filter
text:
Loading the script and styles
add_html_dependency copies the JavaScript and CSS into the site’s site_libs/ folder and links them from the page. The version is part of the folder name there, so it should be kept in step with the manifest.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 99–104
quarto.doc.add_html_dependency({
  name = "issue-comments",
  version = "0.3.0",
  scripts = { "issue-comments.js" },
  stylesheets = { "issue-comments.css" },
})

title: 2. Lua filter
section: Passing the settings to the page
text:
Passing the settings to the page
The settings go into the page’s <head> as a global variable that the script reads when it starts. Encoding them with quarto.json.encode handles quotes and special characters. The extra replacement of </ covers the one case JSON does not: a value such as contact: "</script><script>…" would otherwise end the script tag and let the rest run as HTML.

_extensions/issue-comments/issue-comments.lua, lines 106–109
-- Escape "</" so values cannot close the script tag.
local json = quarto.json.encode(settings):gsub("</", "<\\/")
quarto.doc.include_text("in-header",
  "<script>window.ISSUE_COMMENTS = " .. json .. ";</script>")

title: 5. Apps Script relay
text: The relay is a Google Apps Script web app that you deploy from your own Google account. It receives each comment, checks it, works out which repository it belongs to, and creates the GitHub issue as your GitHub App. One relay serves all your sites. It is the only part that holds a secret, so it is the part to read most carefully.

title: 5. Apps Script relay
text:
Settings
All configuration lives in Script Properties, which only you can see. Changing a property takes effect on the next request, with no redeployment.

apps-script/Code.gs, lines 1–20
/**
 * issue-comments relay: receives a reader's comment from a Quarto page and
 * files it as a GitHub issue, posted by your GitHub App (shown as a bot).
 * One relay serves every site and repository you install the app on. The
 * app's private key stays here, in Script Properties, and is never sent to
 * the browser.
 *
 * Script Properties (Project Settings > Script Properties):
 *   GITHUB_APP_ID   the App ID from the app's settings page
 *   GITHUB_APP_KEY  the app's private key: the whole .pem file, pasted as is
 *   GITHUB_OWNER    your GitHub user name; a page at https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/
 *                   posts to <owner>/<repo>
 *   REPO_MAP        optional JSON for any other site address, e.g.
 *                   {"https://example.org/plan/": "owner/repo"}
 *   PASSCODE        optional, only if you set `passcode: true` in Quarto
 *   LABEL           optional, defaults to "reader-comment"
 *   MAX_PER_HOUR    optional, defaults to 20 for each repository
 *
 * A repository receives comments only if the app is installed on it.
 */

text:
Updating the deployment
After changing Code.gs, use Deploy → Manage deployments → Edit → Version: New version. That keeps the same /exec URL. New deployment gives a new URL, which every site using the relay would then need.

title: issue-comments
text:
issue-comments is a Quarto extension. A reader highlights a passage on your site, types their name and a comment, checks a preview, and clicks Post publicly. The comment becomes an issue in a GitHub repository you choose, with the passage quoted and a link back to its section. Readers need no GitHub account, or any account.
flowchart LR
  A["Reader's browser<br/>(issue-comments.js)"] -- "name, comment,<br/>passage, page" --> B["Google Apps Script<br/>relay (Code.gs)<br/>holds your app's key"]
  B -- "GitHub REST API" --> C["Issue in the page's<br/>repository, by your bot"]
Issues are posted by your own GitHub App, so they show as from a bot rather than from you. Its key stays in an Apps Script project that you own and is never sent to the page. One relay serves all your sites.

title: issue-comments
text:
Using it
Installation walks through the ten-minute setup, with screenshots. In short:
quarto add VagishHemmige/quarto-commenting-extension
then create a GitHub App, deploy apps-script/Code.gs as a web app, and add its URL to _quarto.yml. Every setting is on the Options page.

title: issue-comments
text:
What this site is for
This site explains how the extension works, file by file, for anyone who wants to check it before trusting it with their GitHub account, change it, or contribute. The code on every page is read from the repository’s files when the site is built, so what you see is the code that quarto add installs.

How it works follows one comment from a highlighted passage to a GitHub issue.
Security and privacy sets out what each guard protects against, and what it does not.
The Source code pages take each of the five files in turn, in the order a comment passes through them.

title: issue-comments
text:
Status
Version 0.3.0. Version 0.2.0 was used end to end on a live GitHub Pages site, with comments arriving as issues. 0.3.0 posts as a GitHub App, serves several repositories from one relay, and lets sites change the wording. It has been tested against a stand-in for GitHub but not yet on a live site, and the repository has no automated tests.

title: How it works
text: The extension is five files in three places, and each runs at a different time.

title: How it works
text:
At render time
You turn the extension on by listing issue-comments under filters: and giving it an issue-comments: block in _quarto.yml or a page’s front matter. For each page, the Lua filter:

stops unless the output is HTML and the block has an endpoint;
works out the remaining settings, falling back to the document’s first author for owner, and checks any custom wording;
attaches issue-comments.js and issue-comments.css to the page; and
writes the settings into the page’s <head> as window.ISSUE_COMMENTS.

Nothing is sent anywhere at render time. A page without the block, or a PDF or Word render, is left exactly as it was.

title: How it works
text:
In the reader’s browser





sequenceDiagram
  actor R as Reader
  participant P as Page (issue-comments.js)
  participant S as Apps Script relay
  participant G as GitHub API
  R->>P: highlights text
  P-->>R: shows 💬 Comment beside the selection
  R->>P: clicks it, types name and comment
  P-->>R: shows the exact issue (preview)
  R->>P: Post publicly
  P->>S: POST JSON as text/plain
  S->>S: honeypot, page to repository, hourly, passcode and length checks
  S->>G: app installation on that repository, then a 1-hour token (cached)
  S->>G: POST /repos/owner/repo/issues (as the app's bot)
  G-->>S: 201 Created, issue number and URL
  S-->>P: { ok: true, number, url }
  P-->>R: Thanks! Posted as issue 12






The script watches the selection. When it covers at least two characters inside the page’s main content, it records the text (cut to 1,500 characters), the nearest heading and that section’s id, and places the button under the end of the selection. The dialog has three stages: edit, preview (unless preview: false) and done. The reader’s name is saved in their own browser so they don’t retype it.
The request is sent as text/plain so the browser does not first send a CORS “preflight” request, which Apps Script cannot answer.

title: How it works
text:
On the relay
doPost reads your Script Properties, works out the repository from the page’s address, runs its checks, builds the issue text, and creates the issue as your GitHub App, using a token limited to that repository. Because the repository comes from the page, one relay serves every site whose repository has the app installed. It always answers with JSON of the form { ok, error } or { ok, number, url }, which the page shows to the reader. doGet exists only so that opening the /exec URL in a browser confirms the deployment is live.

title: How it works
section: Two copies of the issue format
text:
Two copies of the issue format
The preview has to show exactly what will be posted, but the issue is built on the relay. So the format is written twice: buildIssue_ in Code.gs, and issueTitle and fillPreview in issue-comments.js. A change to one needs the same change to the other. The relay page lists where the two currently differ.

title: Security and privacy
text: The extension lets anyone who can reach your relay cause your GitHub App to open an issue. This page sets out what limits that, so you can judge whether the limits are enough for your site.

title: Security and privacy
text:
The app’s key
The relay posts as a GitHub App, not as you. Its private key is stored only in the Apps Script project’s Script Properties. The page never receives it: the filter writes only endpoint, owner, contact, three on/off settings and any custom wording into the page, and the relay’s replies contain only ok, error, number and url.
For each comment, the relay uses the key to sign a request that lasts ten minutes, and exchanges it for a GitHub token that lasts an hour and is limited to one repository and to issues. The relay keeps that token in its cache for 50 minutes, so most comments make no extra request.
The relay is deployed to Execute as: Me and Who has access: Anyone, so readers can reach it without signing in. Anyone who finds the /exec URL in your page source can therefore send it requests. What protects you is the app’s scope: Issues: Read and write, and only on the repositories you installed it on. Even if the relay had a bug or the key leaked, the damage is limited to issues in those repositories, posted under the bot’s name. It cannot push code, and it cannot act as you. If the key does leak, delete it on the app’s page. No new tokens can then be made with it, and any already made expire within the hour.

title: Security and privacy
section: Which repository a comment goes to
text:
Which repository a comment goes to
The page reports its own address, and the relay rebuilds it from its parts: https, a host name, and a path in which anything unusual is percent-encoded. A forged address therefore cannot add text or links to the issue. The relay then picks the repository from that address, using REPO_MAP or the <owner>.github.io/<repo>/ rule, and refuses it unless the app is installed there.
The address is still supplied by the sender, so it is not proof of where a request came from. Someone could send a comment that claims to come from one of your sites without visiting it. They could only reach repositories where you installed the app, and only within that repository’s hourly allowance.

title: Security and privacy
text:
Guards on the relay








Guard
Stops
Does not stop




Hidden “website” field (honeypot)
simple bots that fill in every field; they get a fake success
anyone who reads the page’s code


Repository matching, and the app’s installations
comments going to any repository you didn’t install the app on
a hand-made request naming one of your sites


MAX_PER_HOUR (default 20 per repository, over any 60 minutes)
a flood of issues; rapid passcode guessing, since wrong guesses count
a slow trickle; one person using up a repository’s allowance for an hour


PASSCODE (optional)
strangers, if you share it only with intended readers
anyone you’ve told it to; one passcode covers all your sites


Length limits (name 80, comment 5,000, passage about 1,600, page 500 characters)
oversized issues
—


@ mentions, owner/repo#12 references and links to other repositories’ issues defused
comments pinging GitHub users, or adding “mentioned this” to other people’s issues
—



The count lives in Apps Script’s cache, which Google may clear early, so treat the limit as a brake, not a guarantee. If spam does arrive, turn on the passcode, lower MAX_PER_HOUR, uninstall the app from a repository, or close the deployment.

title: Security and privacy
text:
Guards on the page

Everything a reader types, and every setting, including custom wording, is put on the page as text (textContent), never as HTML, so a comment or a setting cannot inject markup.
The contact link is used only if it is an http, https, mailto or relative address, so a javascript: URL in the settings cannot run.
The filter escapes </ in the settings it writes into the page, so a value cannot close the <script> tag early.

title: Security and privacy
text:
What readers’ data goes where
A reader’s name, comment, the highlighted passage, the section heading and anchor, and the page address go to the relay, and from there into a public issue (all except the anchor and page, which form the section link). Their name is also kept in their own browser’s localStorage to save retyping, and the default notice says so. A passcode is sent with each comment and checked, but never stored or posted. Nothing else is collected: no email, no GitHub identity, no cookies. Apps Script does not give the script the reader’s IP address, though Google keeps its own request logs.
Readers are told before posting that the comment is public, who it goes to, and that they cannot edit or delete it themselves; they are shown the exact issue first unless you set preview: false. If you reword the notice with text:, keep those points in it.

title: Security and privacy
section: Limits that follow from the design
text:
Limits that follow from the design

Names are not verified. Anyone with the passcode, or anyone at all if there is none, can type any name.
Comments are posted as typed. GitHub renders Markdown in the comment and passage, so a reader can add links or formatting. The name and section heading are escaped.
Readers are not notified of replies, because they have no GitHub identity in the issue.

title: About
text:
Contributing
Report a problem or suggest a change by opening an issue. Changes reach main through pull requests.
A change to the issue format has to be made in two places, buildIssue_ in apps-script/Code.gs and issueTitle and fillPreview in issue-comments.js; see How it works.

title: About
text:
How this site is built
The site is a Quarto website in the site/ folder of the extension’s repository. _quarto.yml and index.qmd are at the top of that folder and the other pages are in site/quarto/. quarto add copies only _extensions/issue-comments/, so none of the site reaches people who install the extension.
The rendered site is not committed. On every push to main, a GitHub Action (.github/workflows/publish.yml) renders site/ with a pinned Quarto version and publishes the result to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. The Action can also be run by hand from the repository’s Actions tab.
The code on each page is not pasted in. Each block names a file and a line of text it starts at, and a small filter, site-tools/source-snippet.lua, reads those lines from the file when the site is rendered and links them to the same lines on GitHub. If a file is renamed or the starting line changes, the render fails with a message naming the page and file, so the site cannot silently fall out of date. The prose still has to be updated by hand when the code’s behaviour changes, in the same pull request.
To check a change before merging, run quarto render site (or quarto preview site) from the repository’s root; the output goes to site/_site/, which git ignores.

title: 3. Browser script
text: The script runs in the reader’s browser. It shows the 💬 Comment button next to a selection, runs the comment dialog, and sends the comment to the relay. It has no dependencies, and the whole file is wrapped in a function so that nothing except what the filter set (window.ISSUE_COMMENTS) is shared with the page.

title: Options
text:
Page settings
These go in the issue-comments: block in _quarto.yml or a page’s front matter. Only endpoint is required.








Option
Default
What it does




endpoint
(required)
The Apps Script web app URL, ending in /exec. Every site can use the same one.


owner
the document’s first author, else “the site owner”
The name readers are told the issue is posted on behalf of.


contact
none (Quarto warns)
Where readers go to change or remove a comment: a contact page, your GitHub profile, or mailto:you@example.com. Only http, https, mailto and relative links are used.


preview
true
Show readers the exact issue before it posts.


passcode
false
Show a passcode box. Set it when the relay has PASSCODE.


page-button
false
Also show a fixed “Comment on this page” button, for comments not tied to a passage.


text
the wording below
Replace any of the wording readers see.



With the block in _quarto.yml, a single page can opt out with issue-comments: false in its front matter.

title: Options
text:
Wording
Everything readers see can be reworded with text:. Give only the keys you want to change; the rest keep their defaults. Quarto warns about a key it doesn’t recognise.
issue-comments:
  endpoint: https://script.google.com/macros/s/XXXXXXXX/exec
  contact: mailto:jane@example.com
  text:
    heading: Comment on the draft plan
    notice: >-
      This draft is shared with the study team only. Comments are filed as
      GitHub issues for {owner}; to change or remove one, {contact}.
    post: Send to the team
A word in braces is filled in where it appears. {owner} works in every key.







Key
Default




button
💬 Comment


page-button
💬 Comment on this page


heading
Leave a comment


preview-heading
Check before posting


section
Section: {section}


name-label
Your name


comment-label
Comment


passcode-label
Passcode


notice
Comments are posted publicly as GitHub issues on behalf of {owner}, together with your name, the highlighted text and a link to this section. You can’t edit or delete a comment after posting; to change or remove one, {contact}. Your name is saved in this browser so you don’t have to retype it.


contact-link
contact {owner} (the text of the {contact} link)


preview-intro
This is exactly what will be posted publicly on GitHub on behalf of {owner}:


cancel, edit, close
Cancel, Edit, Close


preview, post
Preview, Post publicly


posting
Posting…


thanks
Thanks! Posted as {issue}.


issue-link
issue #{number} (the text of the {issue} link)



Wording is always shown as plain text, so nothing in it can add HTML to the page. Three things are not set here:

The issue itself (title, “Submitted by”, the section link) is written by the relay, so a reader can’t change it, and the preview shows it as it will be.
Error messages, such as “That passcode is not correct”, come from the relay.
The notice should stay true. If you reword it, keep telling readers that comments are public, who receives them, and how to have one removed.

title: Options
text:
Passcode
A passcode keeps commenting to the people you give it to. Set PASSCODE in the relay’s Script Properties, and passcode: true on every site that uses the relay, so readers see the box. One passcode covers all your sites.
Use a long phrase, such as four unrelated words, rather than something memorable. Wrong guesses count against MAX_PER_HOUR, so they can’t be tried quickly, but that also means a run of guesses can use up a site’s allowance for an hour. To change the passcode, change the property; readers aren’t asked to remember it between visits.

title: Options
text:
Relay settings
These are Script Properties in the Apps Script project (Project Settings → Script Properties). A change takes effect on the next comment, with no redeployment.



Property
Default
What it does




GITHUB_APP_ID
(required)
The App ID from your GitHub App’s settings page.


GITHUB_APP_KEY
(required)
The app’s private key: the whole .pem file. Either format GitHub uses is accepted, with or without line breaks.


GITHUB_OWNER
none
Your GitHub user name. A page at https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/… sends its comments to <owner>/<repo>.


REPO_MAP
none
Sites at any other address, as JSON from address to repository. See below.


PASSCODE
none
The passcode readers must enter. See Passcode.


LABEL
reader-comment
The label put on every comment’s issue, so you can filter them.


MAX_PER_HOUR
20
The most comments accepted for one repository in any 60 minutes. Each repository has its own count.



Whichever way a page is matched, a repository only receives comments if the app is installed on it.

REPO_MAP
REPO_MAP covers a site on its own domain, a user site (https://<owner>.github.io/ itself), a site whose comments should go to a different repository, and quarto preview:
{
  "https://plan.example.org/": "VagishHemmige/USRDS",
  "https://vagishhemmige.github.io/HIV-SLK/": "VagishHemmige/HIV-SLK-comments",
  "http://localhost:4200/": "VagishHemmige/test-comments"
}
Each address is the start of the page addresses it covers. When several match, the longest wins, and a match here takes priority over the GITHUB_OWNER rule. Plain http is accepted only for localhost, for previews. quarto preview can pick a different port each time, so give it one with --port 4200.

title: Options
text:
Maintenance
The private key. It doesn’t expire. To replace it, generate a new one on the app’s page, paste it into GITHUB_APP_KEY, and delete the old key on the app’s page. No redeployment is needed.
Adding a site. Install the app on its repository, and give the site the same endpoint. See Adding another site.
Updating the script. After changing Code.gs, use Deploy → Manage deployments → Edit → Version: New version. That keeps the same /exec URL. New deployment gives a new URL, which every page using the relay would then need.
Changing the issue format. The page previews the issue itself, so the format is written twice: buildIssue_ in Code.gs, and issueTitle and fillPreview in issue-comments.js. Change both together. See How it works.
